Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Comoros rural police stations use entirely paper-based recording for case files, complaints, and incident reports. The 2014 Criminal Procedure Code mandates officers draft procès-verbaux (PVs) on-site for all investigations, statements, seizures, and garde à vue; PVs are signed per page, read aloud, and originals physically sent to prosecutors—no digital/electronic methods mentioned. No evidence of digital case management systems, pilots, or digitisation at station level found in national justice site, US State Dept HR reports (2023-2024), UNODC, or OC Index. Justice reforms focus on courts/IT equipment, not police. Francophone procedures confirm handwritten PVs standard in rural posts. Score 1 as paper-mandated, no rural digital evidence.

revision_notes: Confirmed. Original sources (2014 Criminal Procedure Code mandating paper procès-verbaux; US State Dept 2023/2024 HR reports) still apply; no evidence found of digitisation at rural police/gendarmerie station level. A 2025 market report on the Comorian law enforcement software market confirms no case-management or record-management software has yet been adopted nationally, stating that "no specific policies have been enacted" despite ongoing digital transformation initiatives. The Ministry of Justice FAQ page lists numerous rural gendarmerie posts (e.g. Koimbani, Foumbouni, Domoni, Pomoni) with no mention of digital systems. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural police and gendarmerie stations in Comoros record complaints, statements and case files entirely on paper. The 2014 Code of Criminal Procedure requires officers to draft handwritten procès-verbaux for all investigations, which are signed, read aloud and physically forwarded to prosecutors, with no digital or electronic alternative specified. No case-management or records software has been deployed at police or gendarmerie posts: a 2025 industry assessment of the Comorian law-enforcement software market notes that no specific digitisation policies have yet been enacted, notwithstanding a broader $10 million AfDB-backed digital government programme covering biometric identification and e-government portals. Rural gendarmerie brigades, including those at Koimbani, Foumbouni, Domoni and Pomoni, continue to operate without digital record-keeping at the point of service.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Comoros (prefectures and communes, many in rural areas) currently record births using paper-based état civil registers and forms, as indicated by historical records and lack of evidence for electronic entry at point of service.FamilySearch Wiki A 2016 ECA assessment placed Comoros in the lowest category (<35%) for digitization, infrastructure (35-49%), and processes, with regional trends showing most local offices paper-dependent and under-resourced.ECA Report No routine digital systems at rural facilities; completeness low due to rural inaccessibility. Recent developments include a 2023 law mandating computerization and 2026 validation of a nationwide digitization plan (Amecc, funded by France/UNICEF), responding to a 2022 assessment highlighting a "largely manual" system prone to errors and fraud. This remains a national ambition/pilot stage, not deployed at rural points of service.We Are Tech Africa Key barriers: poor infrastructure, limited HR/training, low digital maturity (esp. outer islands), underfunding. Gap: Policy pushes digital ID/CRVS interoperability, but rural reality is entirely paper-based with ad hoc efforts.

revision_notes: Confirmed and refreshed. The 2023 law (n°23-016/AU) mandating computerisation of civil registration remains at the planning stage: preparatory digitisation studies were only validated in Moroni and Mohéli between October 2025 and March 2026 under the AMECC programme (funded by France, with UNICEF technical support), and as of April-May 2026 the government is still drafting the implementing decree for a new National Civil Registration Agency (ANEC) and running capacity-building workshops for registry agents across the islands. No rural civil registry office is yet operating a digital system at point of service; the register remains "largely manual" per the 2022 assessment underpinning the reform. Original sources (APAI-CRVS Africa report, FamilySearch wiki) remain broadly consistent with this. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed, year updated to reflect the latest 2026 evidence.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices across Comoros' prefectures and communes continue to record births, deaths and marriages on paper état civil registers. A 2023 law (n°23-016/AU) mandates eventual computerisation of civil registration, and the government, through the AMECC programme funded by France with UNICEF technical support, validated preparatory digitisation studies in Moroni and Mohéli between October 2025 and March 2026, setting out plans for a unique Personal Identification Number and a new National Civil Registration Agency (ANEC). As of mid-2026 the reform remains at the planning and consultation stage, with implementing decrees still being drafted and agent training workshops under way across the islands; no rural registry office yet captures vital events digitally at the point of service. The reform responds to a 2022 assessment that described the existing system as largely manual and prone to errors, document loss and fraud.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Comoros predominantly use paper-based registers for administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. The national EMIS (SIGE) was designed to collect data from all schools but has been defunct since around 2018 due to funding shortages and complexity, relying on likely manual paper inputs aggregated centrally World Bank 2021 Assessment. Digital infrastructure is minimal: only 30.8% primary schools had computers (2017), 40.9% electricity (2017)/48.4% (2021), and 8% internet (2017)/21.4% (2021), with no rural-urban split but rural areas facing greater disparities in access and infrastructure UNESCO SDG4 Profile. Recent national digital platforms like e-Msomo (launched ~2025, for student records/grades/staff mgmt) and E-Shiyo (online textbooks) exist, supported by UNICEF/ANADEN, but no evidence of routine use at rural point-of-service; low connectivity (35.7% national internet) and hardware limits rollout to pilots or urban. Key barriers: poor infrastructure, electricity/internet deficits, budget dominated by salaries (96-99%), cyclones disrupting data. National ambitions (e.g., digital strategy 2028) outpace rural reality, where paper remains default.

revision_notes: Confirmed, with a caveat flagged for review. Original sources (defunct SIGE EMIS, UNESCO 2017/2021 infrastructure data) still describe minimal ICT access in schools. However, fresh reporting shows the Ministry of Education/ANADEN launched e-Msomo (grade entry, automated report cards) and e-Shiyo (digital textbooks for pre-primary/primary pupils) nationally in June 2025, with e-Msomo reported at around 95% of secondary schools registered by February 2026, including named rural collèges (Domoni, Mboueni) actively entering grades, alongside continued technical and adoption problems (platform migrations, delayed report cards, teacher training gaps). Evidence on uptake within primary schools specifically (as opposed to collèges/lycées) is thin, so it is unclear whether rural PRIMARY schools - the scope of this variable - have moved meaningfully beyond paper registers for day-to-day data capture. Score kept at 1 (Entirely paper) but flagged for human review given the pace of the e-Msomo/e-Shiyo rollout and the risk that this variable now understates the primary-school picture.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Comoros continue to rely on paper-based registers for attendance, grades and administrative records. The national EMIS (SIGE) has been defunct since around 2018, and UNESCO data show only limited ICT infrastructure in primary schools (electricity access around 48%, internet access around 21% as of 2021), with rural schools facing the greatest disparities in access. The Ministry of Education and the National Agency for Digital Development (ANADEN) launched two national digital platforms in June 2025: e-Msomo, for online grade entry, automated report cards and unique student identifiers, and e-Shiyo, a digital textbook library for pre-primary and primary pupils. By early 2026 the ministry reported the large majority of secondary schools registered on e-Msomo, including some rural collèges, though rollout has been accompanied by technical disruptions and uneven teacher readiness. Uptake specifically within rural primary schools remains unconfirmed, and low national internet penetration (around 36%) together with device shortages continues to constrain rollout beyond pilot and secondary-level sites, leaving paper as the default at the point of service for most rural primary schools.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural clinics in Comoros transitioned from paper-based stock and service reporting to DHIS2, used by 99% of public facilities including primaries. 2024 World Bank-funded eLMIS digitized stock management at 78% of 74 facilities via Android RTS tool, replacing handwritten records and enabling real-time data (previously weeks for aggregation) DHIS2. WB COMPASS (2019) notes HMIS DHIS2 upgrade ongoing, but PBF verifies against paper registries/cards; only 14% facilities have computers World Bank. No EMR/patient records found; likely paper at clinic level, digitized aggregates later. Score 2: Predominantly paper, some digital via DHIS2 pilots/projects.

revision_notes: Confirmed and refreshed. DHIS2 remains used by around 99% of public facilities for aggregate health-service reporting, and a 2024 World Bank-funded eLMIS project (using the DHIS2 Real-Time Stock Management tool on Android) had digitised stock-management transactions at 78% of the country's 74 facilities by November 2025, replacing handwritten stock ledgers. A new openIMIS-based health insurance platform (Assurance Maladie Généralisée, AMG) began piloting from December 2025 in Mohéli, digitising enrolment and claims data for around 318,000 people, but this is an insurance/administrative layer rather than clinical record capture at the point of care. No evidence of electronic medical or patient records at rural clinic level was found; routine clinical data capture (consultations, patient notes) remains paper-based, with digital tools confined to stock management, aggregate reporting and, from late 2025, insurance enrolment. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Comoros record most day-to-day clinical data, such as patient consultations and treatment notes, on paper, but several digital layers now operate alongside this. Almost all public health facilities (around 99%) use DHIS2 for routine health-service reporting, and a World Bank-funded eLMIS project introduced an Android-based Real-Time Stock tool in 2024 that had digitised stock-management transactions at 78% of the country's 74 facilities by November 2025, replacing handwritten stock ledgers. From December 2025 a pilot of the openIMIS-based Assurance Maladie Généralisée (AMG) health insurance platform began enrolling beneficiaries and processing claims in Mohéli. These initiatives digitise supply-chain, reporting and insurance data, but there is no evidence of electronic patient records or clinical data capture at the point of care, so clinics remain predominantly paper-based with meaningful but partial digital elements.
